method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: QUOTED from Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI) 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders' (vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024), 16 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11356788 ('open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY) license')). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001) 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)' (first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022), 12 claims; LICENCE: No licence or reproduction permission stated on the portal (disclaimer only); the journal version is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (read at the portal's Disclaimer page (guidelines.php/146/disclaim) and the Elsevier API openaccessUserLicense field for S1096719220302018). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the GMDI/SERN VLCAD nutrition management guideline (v1.4), read on the SERN Management Guidelines Portal: the five Nutrition Recommendations pages (questions 1-5) were fetched and their tables stripped. The journal copy on ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 and was not used. S2 covers VLCAD only, the commonest LC-FAOD. All S1 claims are unchanged; S2 is paraphrased and hash-anchored.

claims.claim: **Symptoms appear with fasting or metabolic stress:** cardiomyopathy, skeletal muscle and/or liver involvement, with neurological effects from hypoglycaemia; between crises patients are often well.
claims.source_text: Characteristically, FAODs in periods of fasting or metabolic decompensation present cardiac myopathy (colloquially referred to as "the machine without petrol") or skeletal and/or hepatic involvement … In inter-crisis periods, they are often found to be asymptomatic.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Frequent meals:** every 3–4 h under 1 year; every 4–5 h over 1 year, never fasting more than 8 h. Never skip breakfast.
claims.source_text: Never skip breakfast. For children under 1 year, meals should be every 3-4 h. For children older than 1 year, meals can be every 4-5 h with never more than 8 h of fasting.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A midnight meal is advisable; uncooked cornstarch can be used from 8 months,** keeping glucose normal for 6–8 h. Start at 1.0–1.5 g/kg and increase gradually to 1.75–2 g/kg by 2 years.
claims.source_text: It is advisable to have a midnight meal. Cornstarch can be used from 8 months of age when the pancreatic enzymes have the optimal capacity for adequate absorption. This preparation has a large amount of branched glucose chains that are hydrolysed and released slowly, allowing normoglycaemia figures to be maintained for 6-8 h … Start with 1.0-1.5 g/kg and gradually increase to 1.75-2 g/kg at 2 years of age.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **With cardiomyopathy or feeding difficulty, consider continuous overnight tube feeding.**
claims.source_text: In severe cases with cardiomyopathy or feeding difficulties, nocturnal continuous enteral feeding by nasogastric tube or gastrostomy should be considered.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Restrict long-chain triglycerides to 10% of total energy;** lower restriction risks essential fatty acid deficiency, higher allows toxic metabolites. Give linoleic acid 3–4% and linolenic acid 0.5–1% of calories.
claims.source_text: Long-chain triglyceride (LCT) restriction to 10% of total energy (normalises plasma acylcarnitines), as restrictions below this figure entail a high risk of essential fatty acid deficiency and higher figures increase their potentially toxic metabolites … Linoleic acid (C18:2n6) and linolenic acid (C18:3n3) intake of 3-4% and 0.5-1%, respectively, of total calories
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Add MCT at 10–25% of total energy (at least 10%);** as pure MCT, 2–3 g/kg/day in the first year and 1–1.25 g/kg/day after 1 year. MCT bypasses the carnitine system and long-chain enzymes. Total MCT + LCT = 20–35% of total energy.
claims.source_text: Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) supplementation at 10-25% of total energy. The minimum amount to be administered is 10%, as lower amounts do not decrease abnormal metabolites … not requiring the carnitine system or long-chain enzymes … Pure form at doses of 2-3 g/kg/day in the first year of life and 1-1.25 g/kg/day in those older than 1 year. … Total MCT+LCT = 20-35% of total energy.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Triheptanoin** (odd-chain triglyceride) has been used in MCT non-responders and naïve patients, with fewer crises, hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis reported; it is FDA-approved from the neonatal period and can cause diarrhoea.
claims.source_text: it has been used on a compassionate basis or in clinical trials in both non-responders to MCT therapy and naïve patients with different LC-FAODs (CACT, CPT I, CPT II, MTP, LCHAD, VLCAD) … describing improvements in quality of life, cardiac function, muscle function and exercise tolerance, with reductions in mortality, time to hospitalisation for crises, number of episodes of hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis. TH has been approved by the FDA and can be administered from the neonatal period, has a good safety profile and in some patients induces diarrhoea (which improves after fractionation of the dose), abdominal pain or vomiting.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Breastfeeding is fine in mild to moderate disease,** topped up with MCT formula case by case; in symptomatic infants consider stopping it because of its fat content.
claims.source_text: In patients with mild to moderate disease, breastfeeding is not contraindicated, but should be supplemented by MCT-added formulas on a case-by-case basis. In symptomatic infants, discontinuation of breastfeeding should be considered, due to its high fat content
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Before exercise** (for muscle pain or rhabdomyolysis), MCT 0.25–0.5 g/kg or carbohydrate 1 g/kg of ideal weight for height 20 min beforehand helps. Monitor essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins.
claims.source_text: Physical exercise: Patients with exercise-induced muscle pain or weakness (rhabdomyolysis) benefit 20 min prior to exercise from MCT at a dose of 0.25-0.5 g/kg of ideal weight for height [,] or carbohydrate at a dose of 1 g/kg of ideal weight for height or a combination of both at a lower dose. … Monitor plasma levels of essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins for risk of deficiency.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Newborn with suspected VLCAD:** begin fasting precautions while the diagnosis is confirmed. A well infant may keep breastfeeding (or take expressed milk) with no MCT, provided the feeding intervals are kept.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Set long-chain fat by severity, keeping total fat (long-chain plus MCT) within the dietary reference intake for age:** mild and symptom-free, no MCT substitution is needed; moderate, long-chain fat at 15 to 30% of estimated energy; severe, 10 to 15%. Going under 10% may add nothing even in severe disease. Then add MCT to make up the total fat.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Breastfeeding by severity:** mild and symptom-free, breast milk without MCT if supply and weight gain are adequate; moderate, breast milk with a possible low long-chain, high-MCT medical food; severe, that medical food as the main nutrition; symptomatic, some breast milk may still be possible. Breastfeeding stopped during a crisis can be partly resumed once the infant is well.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Fasting limits when well:** feeds every 3 to 4 hours for symptom-free newborns; an overnight fast of 8 to 10 hours at 9 to under 12 months; a maximum of 10 to 12 hours after 12 months. Use the shorter end in severe disease.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Uncooked cornstarch at bedtime is not indicated in VLCAD,** because hypoglycaemia is unlikely in a well person who avoids long fasts and meets energy needs; a complex-carbohydrate bedtime snack is preferred, with overnight tube feeds for severe disease if a snack is not enough.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Essential fatty acids:** infants on long-chain restriction with MCT should get a medical food with ARA and DHA. Adjust linoleic acid within 3 to 6% and alpha-linolenic acid within 0.5 to 1.2% of energy against plasma or red-cell profiles; if DHA stays low, supplement 60 mg/day (infants and toddlers) or 100 mg/day (older).
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **During illness:** with acute rhabdomyolysis, lean on carbohydrate (oral or IV) for energy. Prevent crises by spacing meals, keeping people active with extra energy around exercise, and considering a gastrostomy in severe disease with poor intake. Home glucose meters are discouraged, because low glucose is unlikely to be the presenting sign; give families an emergency letter.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In hospital, if intake is inadequate: at least 10% IV dextrose with electrolytes at 1.5 times maintenance or more.** Do not give L-carnitine in acute illness; avoid IV lipids, but supply essential fatty acids after 7 days. Consider a central line in severe disease with frequent admissions.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **L-carnitine when well is probably unnecessary unless free carnitine is below 10 µmol/L;** then start at 10 to 25 mg/kg/day and titrate to levels.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Other treatments (S2):** at the guideline's writing triheptanoin was available only in trials or as an investigational drug, so no general recommendation was made; bezafibrate is experimental and belongs in trials; evidence for CoQ10 and other vitamins is insufficient.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Monitor creatine kinase and the plasma carnitine profile routinely;** add metabolic panel, acylcarnitines, essential fatty acids, fat-soluble vitamins and cardiac checks when circumstances call for it. Confirmatory results (acylcarnitines, genetics, enzyme) help judge severity.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Exercise:** encourage normal activity with energy support. For poor exercise tolerance, give MCT 20 minutes before: 0.1 to 0.3 g/kg of body weight, or 0.25 to 0.5 g/kg of lean mass. Counsel on fluids.
claims.locator: Genetic Metabolic Dietitians International (GMDI) and Southeast Regional Genetics Network (SERN), Management Guidelines Portal; published as Van Calcar SC et al., Mol Genet Metab 2020;131:23-37 (doi 10.1016/j.ymgme.2020.10.001), 'VLCAD Nutrition Management Guidelines (Nutrition management guideline for very-long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency: an evidence- and consensus-based approach)', first edition February 2019, v1.4 updated November 2022, https://southeastgenetics.org/ngp/guidelines.php/146/VLCAD%20Nutrition%20Guidelines, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Any procedure needing fasting (including dental extraction) needs IV 10% glucose before, during and after until feeding is tolerated;** deaths have followed pre-operative fasting in unrecognised FAODs.
claims.source_text: If the patient requires fasting periods for any procedure, including dental extractions, intravenous administration of 10% glucose solution is recommended before, during and after the procedure until feeding is tolerated []. Cases of death have been reported in patients with unrecognised FAODs who have undergone dental extractions and required fasting prior to surgery.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sick day at home:** avoid prolonged fasting, increase carbohydrate quantity and frequency without delay, use the emergency preparation if food is not tolerated, and go to hospital for IV treatment if that fails.
claims.source_text: In stressful situations (infections, fever, vomiting, food refusal, etc.) at home, prolonged fasting should be avoided and a correct caloric intake should be ensured. Parents should be alerted to the need to increase in quantity and frequency the intake of carbohydrates such as fruit, jams, pasta, rice, bread, cornstarch, or gofio, without delaying these measures. … If, despite taking it in small, frequent amounts, it is not tolerated, the patient should go to hospital for intravenous treatment.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Hospital: with vomiting, lethargy or malaise, give 200 mg/kg glucose (2 mL/kg of 10% or 1 mL/kg of 20%) within minutes,** then a maintenance glucose drip for blood glucose 110–120 mg/dL (5–6 mmol/L). Delay can cause sudden death or brain damage.
claims.source_text: If the patient presents with vomiting, lethargy or general malaise, immediately administer 200 mg/kg of glucose (2 mL/kg of 10% glucose or 1 mL/kg of 20% glucose) within a few minutes. Follow with a maintenance glucose drip to ensure adequate blood sugar levels (110-120 mg/dL; 5-6 mmol/L) … Delays in emergency treatment may result in sudden death or permanent brain damage.
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Keep patients well hydrated in rhabdomyolysis to protect the kidneys;** correct acidosis with pH < 7.20 using IV bicarbonate. Carnitine is generally avoided in acute decompensation.
claims.source_text: Hydration is essential during episodes of rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria to prevent renal failure … If metabolic acidosis with pH < 7.20 is present, it should be rapidly corrected with i.v. sodium bicarbonate. … There is no consensus on the use of carnitine in acute decompensation, the current tendency being not to use it
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give patients an emergency letter** for all doctors, especially emergency physicians.
claims.source_text: It is advisable for patients to have an information document (emergency letter) addressed to all physicians, especially emergency physicians
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Carnitine is controversial in LC-FAODs** (toxic long-chain acylcarnitines, linked to ventricular fibrillation and rhabdomyolysis) and may harm in CPT I, CPT II and CACT deficiency; it is essential only in primary carnitine uptake or transport disorders. Consider it cautiously only if levels are low.
claims.source_text: Carnitine: The use of this detoxifier is still controversial, due to the risk of production of long-chain acylcarnitines and their toxic intramitochondrial accumulation, which has been associated with ventricular fibrillation and rhabdomyolysis []. It is absolutely essential in primary carnitine uptake or transport disorders … It may be counterproductive in acylcarnitine transport disorders (CPT I, CPT II and CACT) … It should only be considered and with great caution if carnitine levels are low
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Anaesthesia:** avoid volatile agents, lipid-rich agents such as propofol and etomidate, and muscle relaxants; midazolam, fentanyl, thiopental, sevoflurane and nitrous oxide may be used. Also avoid valproic acid, salicylates, pivalic acid, statins and adrenaline.
claims.source_text: In patients with LC-FAODs, avoid volatile anaesthetics and those containing high doses of long-chain fatty acids such as propofol and etomidate, as well as muscle relaxants. Midazolam, fentanyl, thiopental, sevoflurane and nitrous oxide may be used as anaesthetics. … Pivalic acid, valproic acid, salicylates and acetaminophen due to carnitine consumption. … Statins for increasing OAG. Adrenaline for its lipolytic effect
claims.locator: Peña-Quintana L, Correcher-Medina P, et al., Nutrients (MDPI), 'Nutritional Management of Patients with Fatty Acid Oxidation Disorders', vol. 16, article 2707, published 14 August 2024, https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162707, retrieved 2026-09-23
